events.title: Declaration of Independence Adopted
events.blurb: Delegates from thirteen British colonies voted to ratify a document asserting that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights, formally severing political ties with the Crown. The declaration listed 27 specific grievances against the king; most delegates signed an engrossed parchment copy nearly a month later.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1776 — Philadelphia. Only two men actually signed on the Fourth (Hancock and Thomson). Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams all died on July 4 — Jefferson and Adams on the same day, the 50th anniversary, within hours of each other.

events.title: Treaty of Paris Recognizes American Independence
events.blurb: Representatives of Britain and the United States signed a peace treaty at a Paris hotel ending the American Revolutionary War. Britain recognized the new country's independence; set its western boundary at the Mississippi River; and granted generous fishing rights off Newfoundland. Spain and France signed separate treaties the same day ending their parallel wars. Britain had lost the largest and richest colony in the world.
events.revealBlurb: September 3, 1783 — Hotel d'York, Paris. American negotiators: Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, John Jay. The United States shrewdly kept its French ally out of the negotiations, violating the Franco-American alliance's terms, and secured better borders as a result.

events.title: Haiti Declares Independence
events.blurb: A former slave turned general, addressing a small crowd at a town on a Caribbean island, declared the independence of a new sovereign state that replaced a French sugar colony. It took the name of the original Taíno indigenous word for the island. It was the first independent state in Latin America, the only one to emerge from a successful slave revolt, and the second republic in the Western hemisphere. European powers reacted with diplomatic ostracism; the United States refused recognition for 58 years.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1804 — Jean-Jacques Dessalines at Gonaïves, Haiti. France demanded reparations for "lost property" — 150 million francs — that Haiti finished paying only in 1947. The combination of debt, ostracism, and internal strife has shaped Haitian poverty for two centuries.

events.title: Grito de Dolores
events.blurb: A 57-year-old Catholic priest in a rural Mexican town, learning that a conspiracy of criollo-elite revolutionaries had been uncovered, rang his church bell in the middle of the night to summon his parishioners and call for the overthrow of Spanish colonial rule. He led his ragged army of peasants and mestizos toward the capital; the colonial government crushed them within four months and he was shot. The rebellion he had started, though, continued for 11 more years.
events.revealBlurb: September 16, 1810 — Father Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla at Dolores, Guanajuato. The exact wording of his "grito" is not recorded. Hidalgo was captured in March 1811 and executed by firing squad on July 30, 1811. September 16 is Mexico's Independence Day; the President still rings the bell each year.

events.title: Napoleon Invades Russia
events.blurb: A French emperor crossed the Neman River into Russian territory with the largest army Europe had ever seen — 680,000 men drawn from across his continental empire. His objectives were to compel Russia back into a trade embargo against Britain and to break Russian military power. The Russians fell back, burning as they withdrew, refusing pitched battle. The French reached Moscow in September to find it empty and soon burning. The retreat home through a catastrophic winter would destroy almost the entire army.
events.revealBlurb: June 24, 1812 — the Neman crossing. Of the 680,000 who crossed east, perhaps 40,000 returned. The retreat featured the famous crossing of the Berezina River, where improvised pontoon bridges collapsed under packed refugees; tens of thousands died in the icy water.

events.title: One Thousand and One Nights Compiled
events.blurb: An anonymous Arabic compiler assembled a frame narrative and embedded stories drawn from Persian, Indian, Mesopotamian, and Egyptian sources into a single cycle. The outer frame told of a queen stalling her own execution by telling her king a new story every night; the inner tales — of flying carpets, genies, thieves — became permanent fixtures of world storytelling. The collection continued to accrete new tales for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: c. 10th century CE — the oldest surviving Arabic manuscript dates from the 14th century. "Aladdin," "Ali Baba," and "Sinbad" were added to the collection by an 18th-century French translator, Antoine Galland, working from Syrian oral sources. They are not in the original Arabic canon.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Frankenstein Published
events.blurb: An anonymously published novel telling, through nested letters and narratives, the story of a Swiss medical student who assembles and animates a humanoid creature from stolen body parts. The creature, rejected by its creator, turns on him. The author, a 20-year-old English woman, had dreamed the core story two years earlier during a rainy holiday on Lake Geneva, when her host proposed everyone write a ghost story.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1818 — Mary Shelley (née Godwin), daughter of Mary Wollstonecraft and William Godwin. The Lake Geneva party included Percy Bysshe Shelley, Lord Byron, and John Polidori (whose own contribution became "The Vampyre," the first English-language vampire novel).

events.title: Walden Published
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Massachusetts essayist, graduate of Harvard, former schoolteacher, and occasional pencil-factory worker, published an account of two years and two months he had spent living in a cabin he had built himself beside a glacier-pond near Concord. The book mixed natural observation, economic criticism, and philosophical reflection. It sold slowly; its reputation grew after the author's early death seven years later, and he is now considered one of the founders of American nature writing.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1854 — Henry David Thoreau. He had lived at Walden Pond 1845-47. The pond was, contrary to legend, a short walk from his family home; his mother did his laundry. Thoreau's civil-disobedience essay would later inspire Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.

events.title: War and Peace Published
events.blurb: A 41-year-old Russian aristocrat completed the last serial installment of a vast historical novel following five aristocratic families through Russia's Napoleonic Wars. The finished work ran over 1,200 pages and combined personal drama, military history, and a 200-page essay on the philosophy of history tacked onto the end. The author rewrote the opening sentence at least seven times.
events.revealBlurb: 1869 — Leo Tolstoy. It was serialized in the journal Russky Vestnik between 1865 and 1869. Tolstoy later disowned most of his fiction on religious grounds and decades later attempted to destroy his own estate's copyright to prevent his heirs from profiting.

events.title: Caesar Crosses the Rubicon
events.blurb: A Roman general returning from nine years of conquest in Gaul, forbidden by law from bringing his army across the small river marking the boundary of Italy proper, led a single legion across anyway — knowing the act constituted treason against the Republic. He was reportedly quoting a Greek tragedian: "the die is cast." His subsequent march on Rome ignited a four-year civil war, at the end of which he emerged as a dictator-for-life and the Republic ended in everything but name.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 49 BCE — Julius Caesar with Legion XIII. "Alea iacta est" — "the die is cast" — is attributed to him crossing. The Rubicon itself is a small, easily missable river in northern Italy; its modern identity is still debated by historians. The phrase "crossing the Rubicon" has since become an English idiom.

events.title: Year of the Four Emperors
events.blurb: In a single calendar year, the Roman principate cycled through four rulers — Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and Vespasian — as competing legions backed their own generals in an open civil war. Vespasian, commanding troops in Judaea, won by securing Egypt's grain supply first and strangling Rome's food imports until the Senate gave in.
events.revealBlurb: 69 CE. Otho lost one battle, decided he didn't want more Romans to die for him, and stabbed himself — widely praised as his most noble act. Vitellius, who followed, spent his months in power eating. He was eventually dragged through Rome, publicly mocked, killed, and thrown in the Tiber.

events.title: Colosseum Opens
events.blurb: Emperor Titus inaugurated the newly completed Flavian Amphitheatre with 100 days of continuous spectacles: gladiatorial combat, wild-beast hunts, and a mock naval battle staged inside a flooded arena floor. Over 9,000 wild animals were killed; the building seated between 50,000 and 80,000 spectators and had an awning system rigged by sailors from the Roman fleet.
events.revealBlurb: 80 CE. The Colosseum was built partly with the spoils of Jerusalem, including the great seven-branched menorah from the Temple, carried in the triumphal procession. Vespasian funded it on the same land where Nero had built his private "Golden House," a pointed public-relations gesture.

events.title: The Antonine Plague
events.blurb: Soldiers returning from campaigns in Parthia brought a disease — almost certainly smallpox — that spread from the eastern frontier through every province of the empire over fifteen years. The physician Galen, the most famous doctor of his age, documented symptoms in detail from Rome itself; at the plague's peak witnesses recorded 2,000 deaths per day in the capital alone.
events.revealBlurb: 165–180 CE. Galen's treatment recommendation included keeping patients warm and feeding them milk — the best care available, and completely ineffective. The plague killed co-emperor Lucius Verus in 169 CE and may have killed up to 10% of the empire's total population.

events.title: Aurelian Reunifies the Empire
events.blurb: After the empire had fractured into three competing states, Emperor Aurelian defeated the Palmyrene Empire in the east — capturing its queen Zenobia — and then the breakaway Gallic Empire in the west, bringing Britain, Gaul, Spain, Syria, and Egypt back under a single ruler within five years of taking power. He then began building a massive new defensive wall around Rome itself.
events.revealBlurb: 274 CE. Queen Zenobia of Palmyra had claimed descent from Cleopatra and ruled a sophisticated court of scholars and poets while commanding legions across the Near East. After capture she was eventually settled near Tivoli and, according to some sources, married a Roman senator.

events.title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
events.blurb: An English writer who had been educating herself in French enlightenment philosophy published a 300-page treatise arguing that women appeared inferior only because they received inferior education, and that a rational republic required the rational education of both sexes. It was attacked, praised, and influential on both sides of the Atlantic. She died five years later from complications after childbirth.
events.revealBlurb: January 1792 — Mary Wollstonecraft. The child she died giving birth to was Mary Shelley, author of Frankenstein. Her husband, William Godwin, published an honest memoir after her death that destroyed her reputation for a century.

events.title: Amelia Earhart Solos the Atlantic
events.blurb: A 34-year-old American aviator landed her red single-engine Lockheed Vega in a farmer's meadow in northern Ireland after a 15-hour, 3,260-kilometre flight from Newfoundland, becoming the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic. The trip had included an altimeter failure, engine icing, and a broken exhaust manifold that spewed flames into the cockpit for the last eight hours.
events.revealBlurb: May 20-21, 1932 — exactly five years after Charles Lindbergh's crossing. Earhart had originally meant to land in Paris; she turned toward the nearest pasture when she smelled fuel. She had been the first woman to cross the Atlantic by air four years earlier, but only as a passenger.

events.title: The Feminine Mystique Published
events.blurb: A former labour journalist who had been writing articles for women's magazines published a 410-page book analyzing what she called "the problem that has no name" — the stifling dissatisfaction of educated suburban housewives. It sold three million copies within three years and became the foundational text of a resurgent American feminist movement that would transform employment law, education policy, and reproductive rights.
events.revealBlurb: February 19, 1963 — Betty Friedan. The book drew on her research into a Smith College alumni survey. Friedan went on to co-found the National Organization for Women in 1966 and help lead the 1970 Women's Strike for Equality.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: Kamala Harris Becomes VP
events.blurb: A 56-year-old U.S. senator from California, whose mother had immigrated from India and father from Jamaica, was sworn in on the steps of the U.S. Capitol as the nation's 49th vice president, the first woman, first African-American, and first Asian-American to hold the office. She was sworn in by the first Latina Supreme Court justice, on two bibles: one from Justice Thurgood Marshall's widow and one from a close family friend.
events.revealBlurb: January 20, 2021 — sworn in by Justice Sonia Sotomayor. The inauguration, held two weeks after the January 6 Capitol attack, proceeded behind 25,000 National Guard troops. Harris later became the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee after Joe Biden withdrew.

events.title: September 11 Attacks
events.blurb: Nineteen hijackers affiliated with al-Qaeda commandeered four commercial airliners on a Tuesday morning, crashing two into the twin towers of a Manhattan financial complex, one into a Pentagon wing, and one into a Pennsylvania field after passengers fought back. Both World Trade Center towers collapsed within two hours. 2,977 people died. The attacks reshaped American foreign policy, launched two wars that lasted the next two decades, and redefined commercial aviation security for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 2001 — orchestrated by Osama bin Laden. United States entered Afghanistan in October 2001 and Iraq in March 2003. The 9/11 Memorial & Museum opened on the site in 2014; One World Trade Center, topped out in 2013, is the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere.

events.title: Janet Jackson Super Bowl Halftime
events.blurb: An American pop singer, performing with Justin Timberlake at a Super Bowl halftime show, experienced a "wardrobe malfunction" — Timberlake pulled at her leather bustier at the end of their duet, exposing her right breast for 9/16ths of a second on live television. The incident produced an estimated $550,000 in regulatory fines, congressional hearings, and a lawsuit that reached the Supreme Court. It effectively launched YouTube (co-founder Jawed Karim said later that the desire to re-watch the moment inspired the site). Timberlake's career was barely touched; Jackson's was permanently diminished.
events.revealBlurb: February 1, 2004 — Super Bowl XXXVIII halftime show in Houston. The word "wardrobe malfunction" entered the English language. A 2020 retrospective documentary drew new attention to how asymmetrically the American public had blamed Jackson.

events.title: Balloon Boy Hoax
events.blurb: A Colorado family reported that their 6-year-old son had been carried aloft in a homemade silver mylar weather balloon that had drifted off from their backyard. National news networks covered the balloon's two-hour, 80-kilometre flight live, interrupting regular programming. The balloon landed empty. The boy was found hiding in the family attic. Within a day, the father admitted the whole thing had been a publicity stunt, hoping to land the family a reality-TV show.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2009 — Heene family, Fort Collins, CO. The father Richard Heene was convicted of a felony and served 30 days; the mother Mayumi got misdemeanor charges. The Heenes reportedly received a pardon from Colorado governor Jared Polis in December 2020.

events.title: Whitney Houston Dies
events.blurb: A 48-year-old American singer with one of the most powerful voices in pop music history was found unresponsive in a bathtub at a Beverly Hills hotel. The cause of death was accidental drowning complicated by heart disease and cocaine use. She had been scheduled to attend a Grammy Awards pre-party that evening. Her death came the night before the Grammys themselves, which had to be hastily rewritten to include a tribute. Seven years later her only daughter would die under similar circumstances.
events.revealBlurb: February 11, 2012 — Whitney Houston at the Beverly Hilton. Daughter Bobbi Kristina Brown, 22, was found unresponsive in a bathtub on January 31, 2015 and died six months later. Houston's "I Will Always Love You" had been the bestselling single by a woman in history until Adele surpassed it.

events.title: David Bowie Dies
events.blurb: A 69-year-old English singer and songwriter died of liver cancer at his New York apartment, two days after releasing what turned out to be his final studio album. The album's cover art, title ("Blackstar"), and lyrics — which in retrospect clearly addressed death — had been a farewell that almost nobody had caught in real time. His decades of genre-shifting personas, starting with the glam-rock Ziggy Stardust in 1972, had made him one of the most influential musicians of the late 20th century. His death prompted an international wave of mourning.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 2016 — David Bowie (David Robert Jones). Diagnosed 18 months earlier; kept the illness private. His final public appearance was at the premiere of his off-Broadway musical "Lazarus" in December 2015. 2016 became known as a year of many significant music deaths.

events.title: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion Published
events.blurb: A German mathematician published two laws describing how planets orbit the Sun: first, that orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus; second, that a line from the planet to the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times — meaning planets move faster when close to the Sun. A third law, relating orbital period to distance, followed ten years later, providing the first precise mathematical description of the solar system.
events.revealBlurb: 1609 (laws 1&2) and 1619 (law 3) — Johannes Kepler derived the laws from the most precise observational data in the world, collected by Tycho Brahe. Brahe had guarded the data obsessively and refused to share it; Kepler obtained it only after Brahe's sudden death. He later calculated that Brahe may have died from a burst bladder after refusing to leave a banquet to use the lavatory.

events.title: On the Origin of Species Published
events.blurb: A 502-page book argued that all species of life descended from common ancestors through a process of natural selection, where individuals with heritable traits better suited to their environment survived and reproduced at higher rates. The first print run of 1,250 copies sold out to booksellers on the day it was offered for sale.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1859 — Darwin had sat on the theory for twenty years, terrified of the controversy. He finally rushed it to press only after Alfred Russel Wallace independently wrote him a letter describing the same mechanism. The two men's papers were presented jointly to the Linnean Society in 1858.

events.title: Continental Drift Hypothesis Presented
events.blurb: A German meteorologist proposed that Earth's continents were once joined in a single supercontinent that had since broken apart and drifted slowly across the ocean floor, citing the geometric fit of coastlines, matching fossil records on opposite sides of the Atlantic, and ancient glacial scour marks in tropical regions. The geological community's response was immediate and largely hostile.
events.revealBlurb: January 6, 1912 — Alfred Wegener's hypothesis was mocked at a major American geological meeting in 1926, where a speaker suggested geologists should "be instantly prepared to disregard" it. Wegener died on a Greenland expedition in 1930. The mechanism he was missing — seafloor spreading — was found by Harry Hess in the 1960s.

events.title: Plate Tectonics Theory Accepted
events.blurb: After decades of ridicule, a theory holding that Earth's crust is fractured into massive slabs drifting centimetres each year was vindicated by magnetic stripe patterns mapped on either side of mid-ocean ridges. The pattern matched predictions for seafloor spreading, explaining continental shapes, mountain ranges, and earthquake zones in a single framework.
events.revealBlurb: 1967–68 — the "plate tectonics revolution". Alfred Wegener had proposed continental drift in 1912 and been mocked for it; he died in 1930 on an expedition in Greenland. Geologists officially accepted his core idea thirty-seven years after his death.

events.title: Human Genome Project Completed
events.blurb: An international consortium announced the completion of a map of the entire 3-billion-letter chemical sequence of human DNA, covering 99 percent of gene-containing regions at 99.99 percent accuracy — two years ahead of schedule. The project, begun in 1990, required coordinating laboratories across six countries and produced a reference sequence that has underpinned virtually every major advance in genetic medicine since.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 2003 — a rival private effort by Celera Genomics, led by Craig Venter, raced the public consortium and forced both teams to declare a joint "completion" in 2000. The actual finished sequence was only completed in 2003. A truly gapless human genome wasn't assembled until 2022, when long-read sequencing technology filled the remaining 8%.

events.title: Watt's Separate Condenser Patent
events.blurb: A Scottish instrument maker received a patent for a steam engine design that used a separate condenser chamber, dramatically reducing fuel consumption. Unlike earlier designs that wasted energy reheating the main cylinder on every stroke, the new engine converted roughly 75% more heat into mechanical work.

events.title: Watt's Separate Condenser
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Scottish instrument maker, repairing a model of a 50-year-old atmospheric engine for a university natural philosophy class, realized its efficiency was fatally compromised by repeatedly heating and cooling the same cylinder. His solution — a separate condensing vessel — cut fuel consumption by 75 percent. Patented four years later, the improved engine could be sited anywhere, not only beside a coal pit, and became the prime mover of 19th-century industry.
events.revealBlurb: 1765 insight; January 5, 1769 patent — James Watt. His decade-long partnership with Birmingham industrialist Matthew Boulton commercialized the engine. The unit of power is named for him. "Horsepower" was also his invention, a marketing metric.

events.title: Peterloo Massacre
events.blurb: A crowd of perhaps 60,000 people had gathered on a large open field in a northern English mill city to hear speakers demand parliamentary reform. Local magistrates ordered mounted cavalry to arrest the lead speaker and charge into the crowd. Eighteen people were killed — including a two-year-old child — and hundreds injured. The incident, sardonically named after the Battle of Waterloo four years earlier, became a rallying point for British reform movements for decades.
events.revealBlurb: August 16, 1819 — St Peter's Field, Manchester. The press-blackened newspaper of the day printed the event in black-bordered pages. Shelley wrote "The Mask of Anarchy" in response; it was not published until 1832 out of fear of prosecution. The Peterloo Memorial in Manchester was unveiled in 2019.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Ford Model T Goes on Sale
events.blurb: An American automaker released a new car designed to be cheap, simple to drive, and reliable on the rutted rural roads of the era. It sold for $850 — about half the price of the cheapest competitor. Over 19 years of production, the company would build 15 million of them, mostly painted black because that paint dried fastest. At peak production, a completed Model T rolled off the line every 24 seconds.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1908 — Ford Motor Company. The 1913-1914 introduction of the moving assembly line cut the Model T's price to $490. Henry Ford doubled the minimum wage at his Highland Park plant to $5 a day in January 1914, partly to cut turnover caused by the line's brutal monotony.

events.title: Kismet Released
events.blurb: A Bombay Talkies crime film with an unambiguous anti-hero — the lead character is a thief and a cad — opened in the depths of winter during a bitter internal dispute that was tearing the studio apart, yet became the first film in Indian cinema history to gross ₹1 crore. At a Calcutta cinema it ran for 187 consecutive weeks, a record that stood for 32 years.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 1943, Bombay. Directed by Gyan Mukherjee, starring Ashok Kumar. Its patriotic song "Door Hato Ae Duniyawalon" — aimed at colonial occupation without naming it — spread through cities as independence agitation intensified. The British censors initially approved it without grasping the subtext.

events.title: First Filmfare Awards Ceremony
events.blurb: A British-origin film magazine inaugurated India's first popular film awards at Bombay's Metro Theatre with only five categories, winners chosen through postal ballot by readers, and a chief guest who was the US Ambassador to India. The trophy — a black-painted female figure — later became among the most recognisable objects in the entire industry and came to be known, simply, as the Black Lady.
events.revealBlurb: March 21, 1954 — then called the "Clare Awards" after a recently deceased film critic. Best Film went to Bimal Roy's Do Bigha Zamin; Dilip Kumar won Best Actor for Daag. The ceremony's postal-ballot system meant the public, not critics, decided the winners — a populist structure the awards kept for decades.

events.title: Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge Released
events.blurb: A romance about two Non-Resident Indians falling in love on a Eurorail trip before battling parental disapproval opened in Bombay that autumn and never fully left: it ran continuously at one Mumbai cinema for over two decades, setting a record no Indian film has matched. Its climactic train-platform scene became shorthand for every subsequent Bollywood love story.
events.revealBlurb: October 20, 1995 — Aditya Chopra's directorial debut, age 23. He refused to watch the film with an audience for years. Shah Rukh Khan initially had reservations about the role. The film ran at Mumbai's Maratha Mandir theatre without interruption until 2023 — 1,278 weeks.

events.title: Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai Released
events.blurb: A double-role romantic thriller built around a completely unknown actor — son of its director — became the highest-grossing Hindi film of the year and won 92 awards across ceremonies, a figure the Guinness World Records certified as a record for any single film. The overnight stardom it generated was so total that magazine covers, television specials, and public hysteria followed within days.
events.revealBlurb: January 14, 2000 — directed by Rakesh Roshan, launching his son Hrithik. The film began production before Hrithik had done a single screen test beyond his father's living room. His dancing in the title track introduced a new male movement vocabulary to Bollywood that choreographers have referenced ever since.

events.title: Baahubali: The Conclusion Released
events.blurb: The sequel to a Telugu fantasy epic that had left an entire nation debating one question — "Kattappa ne Baahubali ko kyun mara?" — opened to the largest advance booking in Indian cinema history, sold over 10 million tickets in its first weekend, and earned ₹1,000 crore net in India faster than any film before it, definitively crossing the barrier that only Hindi cinema had previously approached.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 2017 — directed by S.S. Rajamouli. The two-part production cost ₹430 crore, still the most expensive Indian film made at the time. The "why" answer to the Kattappa question — withheld for two years — turned its release into a cultural event rather than just a premiere.

events.title: Turing's Computable Numbers
events.blurb: A 23-year-old British mathematician submitted a paper describing a hypothetical abstract machine — an infinite tape with a movable read/write head obeying a simple finite rule table — that could in principle compute anything a human mathematician could work out by following a procedure. The paper was intended to settle a famous open problem in formal logic; along the way it laid the mathematical groundwork for general-purpose computing.
events.revealBlurb: 1936 — Alan Turing, "On Computable Numbers." Written while he was a 23-year-old student. Turing worked with a physical analogue of the machine at Bletchley Park during WWII to break German Enigma ciphers. He was chemically castrated for homosexuality and died in 1954, probably by suicide.

events.title: Transistor Invented
events.blurb: Three physicists at an American industrial research laboratory demonstrated a working point-contact transistor — a tiny semiconductor device made from germanium that could amplify electrical signals without the vacuum tubes, heat, and bulk then required. Within a decade the invention had reshaped electronics; within five decades, billions of its descendants would fit on a single silicon chip smaller than a fingernail.
events.revealBlurb: December 23, 1947 — John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley at Bell Labs. They shared the 1956 Nobel. Shockley's later semiconductor company, though commercially a failure, seeded Silicon Valley through the departure of its "Traitorous Eight" founders of Fairchild Semiconductor.

events.title: Apple II Released
events.blurb: A young Californian computer company released their second machine — and the first mass-market personal computer designed for non-hobbyists, with built-in color graphics, a working keyboard, a plastic case, and the ability to display text and graphics simultaneously. It shipped for $1,298 and found a broad market among small businesses, schools, and households. Apple's revenues grew 700 percent a year for five consecutive years.
events.revealBlurb: June 10, 1977 — Apple Computer. Engineered largely by Steve Wozniak. The arrival of VisiCalc two years later made it the first computer that small businesses felt they had to buy. Apple sold over 5 million Apple IIs before discontinuing the line in 1993.

events.title: iPod Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company released a white portable music player with a 5 GB hard drive — "1,000 songs in your pocket," according to its co-founder's introduction — and a scrollwheel for navigation. The industry press was unimpressed; smaller MP3 players already existed. Over the next decade, the iPod and its derivatives would sell over 400 million units, reshape the music industry, and serve as a forerunner and technological foundation for the iPhone.
events.revealBlurb: October 23, 2001 — Apple iPod. Steve Jobs introduced it at a small press event, not to a large keynote crowd. Initial reviews focused on how it was Mac-only; the 2003 Windows version opened the floodgates.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: Pasteur's Rabies Vaccine Used on a Human
events.blurb: A French chemist administered the first human dose of an experimental rabies treatment to a nine-year-old boy who had been severely bitten by a rabid dog two days earlier and faced certain death without intervention. The boy survived, and the successful case launched the practice of post-exposure vaccination for infectious disease.

events.title: Pasteur's Rabies Vaccine
events.blurb: A 62-year-old French chemist, who had been working for years on vaccines against animal diseases, administered his experimental rabies vaccine — desiccated spinal cord tissue from infected rabbits — to a 9-year-old Alsatian boy who had been savaged by a rabid dog two days earlier. The boy received 13 injections over ten days and survived. Rabies, previously universally fatal once symptoms appeared, now had an effective post-exposure prophylaxis.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 1885 — Louis Pasteur; patient was Joseph Meister. Pasteur was not licensed as a physician; he could have been prosecuted if the boy had died. Meister grew up, became the gatekeeper at the Institut Pasteur, and is said to have killed himself in 1940 rather than let Nazi troops enter Pasteur's tomb (disputed; he may have died from gas poisoning unrelated).

events.title: Insulin Administered to a Patient
events.blurb: A 14-year-old diabetic patient near death at a Toronto hospital received an injection of pancreatic extract prepared by two medical researchers after earlier formulations had failed due to impurities. The boy recovered, and researchers moved ward to ward injecting the remaining diabetic patients — transforming a death sentence into a manageable condition within weeks.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: Sulfa Drugs Discovered
events.blurb: A German pathologist at a pharmaceutical company, testing a red industrial dye for antibacterial properties, demonstrated that mice injected with streptococci and then treated with the dye survived while untreated mice died. The active ingredient, sulphanilamide, was the first practical antibiotic. It saved millions of lives before being partially displaced by penicillin in the 1940s. The researcher's own daughter was among the first human patients cured — of a streptococcal infection that had been expected to kill her.
events.revealBlurb: January 1935 — Gerhard Domagk at Bayer, testing Prontosil. He won the 1939 Nobel but was forbidden by the Nazi government to accept it; he received the medal after the war in 1947. His daughter Hildegarde had cut her finger; Domagk injected her with Prontosil in desperation and saved her arm.

events.title: Battle of New Orleans
events.blurb: General Andrew Jackson's patchwork army of Tennessee frontiersmen, Louisiana militia, free Black soldiers, Choctaw warriors, and pirates under Jean Lafitte decisively routed an 8,000-strong British force attempting to seize New Orleans, killing or wounding roughly 2,000 redcoats while suffering fewer than 70 American casualties. The lopsided victory made Jackson a national hero and propelled him to the presidency.
events.revealBlurb: January 8, 1815 — Chalmette, Louisiana. The Treaty of Ghent ending the War of 1812 had been signed 15 days earlier — news hadn't arrived. The battle had zero effect on the war's official outcome but enormous effect on American mythology and Jackson's political career.

events.title: Haymarket Bombing, Chicago
events.blurb: At a labor rally in Chicago's Haymarket Square called to protest the police killing of striking workers the previous day, an unknown person threw a dynamite bomb into a column of police officers, killing seven officers and at least four civilians in the ensuing explosion and gunfire. The incident became the defining trauma of American labor radicalism and led to the hanging of four men for conspiracy, despite the bomber's identity never being established.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1886 — Haymarket Square, Chicago. Nobody has ever been identified as the bomber. Governor John Altgeld pardoned the surviving defendants in 1893, calling the trial a miscarriage of justice — and was destroyed politically for it. The date May 4 became International Workers' Day in much of the world as a result of the Haymarket executions.

events.title: Spanish-American War Declaration
events.blurb: The United States declared war on Spain following the mysterious explosion of the battleship USS Maine in Havana Harbor and years of lurid coverage of Spanish atrocities in Cuba by the American yellow press. The 114-day conflict ended Spanish colonial rule in Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines, and announced the United States as a Pacific and Caribbean imperial power.
events.revealBlurb: April 25, 1898 — Washington, D.C. Theodore Roosevelt resigned as Assistant Secretary of the Navy to lead the volunteer Rough Riders cavalry regiment, charging up San Juan Hill — a battle that took one afternoon and made him president. Secretary of State John Hay called it "a splendid little war."

events.title: Apollo 11: First Humans on the Moon
events.blurb: At 10:56 pm EDT that evening, astronaut Neil Armstrong stepped off the lunar module Eagle onto the surface of the Moon and became the first human being to walk on another world, watched live by an estimated 600 million people — roughly one-fifth of humanity. Buzz Aldrin joined him 19 minutes later; the two planted an American flag, collected samples, and departed after 2 hours and 31 minutes on the surface.
events.revealBlurb: July 20, 1969 — Sea of Tranquility, the Moon. Armstrong's famous line was supposed to be "one small step for a man" — he swears he said it; the transmission dropped the "a." Michael Collins orbited alone overhead for 21 hours while his crewmates were on the surface. President Nixon had a speechwriter prepare a statement in case they didn't make it back.

events.title: January 6: U.S. Capitol Attacked
events.blurb: That morning, a mob of several thousand supporters of President Donald Trump stormed the U.S. Capitol building, breaching the chambers and offices of Congress as legislators were in the process of certifying the Electoral College results of the 2020 presidential election. The attack — the first violent breach of the Capitol since British forces burned it in 1814 — resulted in five deaths on the day and led to Trump's second impeachment.
events.revealBlurb: January 6, 2021 — Washington, D.C. Over 1,200 people were charged with crimes related to the attack, the largest criminal investigation in U.S. Justice Department history. Congress completed the electoral certification at 3:44 am the following morning. The Capitol had not been occupied by hostile forces since August 24, 1814.

events.title: Bronze Age Collapse
events.blurb: Across about fifty years, a cascade of interconnected catastrophes destroyed or severely damaged every major Mediterranean and Near Eastern civilization — the Hittite Empire vanished, Mycenaean Greece fell to nothing, Egyptian trade and prestige collapsed, the palatial economies of Cyprus and the Levant burned. The causes remain debated: mysterious "Sea Peoples" migrations, earthquakes, drought, famine, iron weapons disrupting bronze-based warfare. Writing itself was forgotten in several regions for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1200-1150 BCE — affected every major eastern Mediterranean civilization. The Greek "Dark Age" that followed lasted some 400 years; the Mycenaean script Linear B was lost until it was deciphered in 1952. The classical-Greek cultural explosion from 800 BCE was, in a sense, a reboot.

events.title: Peloponnesian War Begins
events.blurb: Tensions between a democratic maritime empire led by Athens and an aristocratic land-based league led by Sparta erupted into open war when Spartan forces invaded Athenian-allied territory. The war would last 27 years, consume Greek wealth, shatter Athenian power, and undermine Greek confidence in the democratic project. A historian who had commanded an Athenian force early in the war produced a narrative account considered a founding masterpiece of Western historiography.
events.revealBlurb: 431 BCE — Athens vs. Sparta. The historian was Thucydides. A plague in 430 BCE killed perhaps a quarter of the Athenian population, including the city's leader Pericles. Athens finally surrendered in 404 BCE after its fleet was destroyed at Aegospotami; Socrates was executed in Athens five years later.

events.title: Julius Caesar Assassinated
events.blurb: A Roman dictator, having been named dictator-for-life a month earlier, was stabbed 23 times by a group of 60 senators at a meeting of the Senate held in a Pompey-built theatre. The assassins, styling themselves "Liberators," had convinced themselves that removing the man who had effectively ended the Republic would restore it. Instead, his death plunged Rome into 14 more years of civil war, at the end of which his adopted heir emerged as the first Roman emperor in all but name.
events.revealBlurb: March 15, 44 BCE — the Ides of March. Conspirators included Brutus and Cassius. The supposed last words "Et tu, Brute?" come from Shakespeare; Caesar's actual last words — if he spoke any — may have been the Greek "kai su, teknon?" ("you too, my child?"). His heir Octavian defeated the conspirators at Philippi two years later.

events.title: Augustus Becomes Emperor
events.blurb: The Roman Senate formally voted a new series of titles and powers to the victor of the civil wars that had ended the Republic — including "Augustus" (the revered), "Princeps" (first citizen), and various senatorial and tribunicial powers. The Republic's forms were maintained — the Senate met, consuls were elected — but real power now flowed through the man at the top. The Roman Empire had begun. Its first emperor would reign 41 years and die of natural causes in his 75th year.
events.revealBlurb: January 16, 27 BCE — Octavian accepts the title "Augustus." He preferred the title "Princeps"; only later emperors would unambiguously style themselves "Imperator." The month August is named for him. He outlived his designated heirs repeatedly; his step-son Tiberius eventually succeeded him in 14 CE.

events.title: Sack of Rome by the Visigoths
events.blurb: A Visigothic king and his army, frustrated by failed negotiations with a Western Roman emperor for lands and subsidies, entered Rome itself through an unguarded gate and spent three days pillaging. It was the first time the city had been sacked since the Gauls in 390 BCE — eight centuries earlier. The city's wealth and status had made it symbolically untouchable; the shock rippled through the Mediterranean world. Pagans blamed Rome's adoption of Christianity; Augustine wrote "The City of God" partly in response.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 410 CE — Alaric I the Visigoth. The emperor Honorius was safely in Ravenna, the western capital since 402. The historian Jerome wrote from Bethlehem: "The city which had taken the whole world was itself taken." Alaric died of illness a few months after the sack.

events.title: Columbus Makes Landfall
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator commanding three vessels landed on an island in the present-day Bahamas after 70 days at sea, believing he had reached islands off the coast of Asia. He planted a royal standard, claimed the land in the name of the Spanish Crown, and named the island San Salvador — its indigenous inhabitants called it Guanahani.

events.title: First Circumnavigation Complete
events.blurb: The last seaworthy ship of a Spanish expedition that had set out three years earlier with five vessels dropped anchor in the Guadalquivir River in Spain — the first ship ever to return to its port of departure after sailing completely around the world. Of the 270 men who had departed, 18 returned alive. Its captain, though no longer the expedition's original commander — who had been killed in the Philippines — had personally sailed the ship the entire way home.
events.revealBlurb: September 6, 1522 — Juan Sebastián Elcano aboard the Victoria. The voyage proved the earth was circumnavigable, and also forced the first adjustment of the ship's log by a day (a precursor to the concept of the International Date Line). Elcano himself died at sea in 1526, three ships into another expedition.

events.title: Edict of Nantes
events.blurb: The first Bourbon king of France, a former Protestant who had converted to Catholicism to secure his crown ("Paris is worth a Mass"), issued an edict guaranteeing Protestant Huguenots freedom of worship in specific towns, civil equality, and the right to maintain their own fortified places. The compromise ended 36 years of Wars of Religion and was the most expansive grant of religious toleration any European state had yet made. His grandson would revoke it 87 years later.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1598 — Henry IV of France. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685, triggering a Protestant exodus of perhaps 400,000 skilled workers. Henry IV himself was assassinated by a Catholic fanatic in 1610.

events.title: Galileo's Telescope Observations
events.blurb: A 46-year-old Paduan university mathematics professor, having improved the magnification of a newly invented Dutch optical toy from 3x to 30x, pointed his telescope at the night sky. Over the following months he observed craters on the moon, four previously unknown moons circling Jupiter, phases of Venus, and individual stars resolvable in the milky white band of the Milky Way. His findings, published in a short Latin book, transformed astronomy.
events.revealBlurb: January 7, 1610 — Galileo Galilei observed Jupiter's moons from Padua. His book "Sidereus Nuncius" (The Starry Messenger) was rushed into print in March. The phases of Venus, observed later that year, were decisive evidence against the Ptolemaic earth-centered model.

events.title: Charles I Beheaded
events.blurb: An English king, convicted of high treason by a specially-convened parliamentary court after losing two civil wars against his own Parliament, was beheaded outside a London banqueting house on a platform erected for the purpose, watched by a large silent crowd. He wore two shirts to keep from shivering in the cold, lest witnesses think him afraid. It was the first judicial execution of a reigning European monarch. Eleven years of republican Commonwealth followed before his son was restored to the throne.
events.revealBlurb: January 30, 1649 — Charles I outside Whitehall Palace. The executioner wore a mask and wig; his identity has never been confirmed. Oliver Cromwell would dominate the subsequent Commonwealth; his corpse was dug up and symbolically "executed" in 1661 after the restoration.

events.title: Nalanda University Founded
events.blurb: A Buddhist monastic complex in a region that is now Bihar became a formally organized university with nine million volumes, 10,000 resident students from Korea, Indonesia, Turkey, and China, and faculty lecturing in eight subjects. Funded by the revenues of 100 villages granted by the Gupta emperor, it operated continuously for seven centuries and was the largest residential educational institution in the ancient world.
events.revealBlurb: c. 427 CE — Gupta era, Bihar. Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang studied there for five years and left the most detailed surviving account. When Bakhtiyar Khilji burned it in 1193, monks fleeing the smoke carried surviving texts across the Himalayas — that's how much of Buddhism survives in Tibet today.

events.title: Vasco da Gama Lands at Calicut
events.blurb: A Portuguese fleet rounded the tip of Africa and crossed the Indian Ocean, arriving at the most important spice port on the Malabar Coast. The Zamorin of Calicut received the visitors politely until he saw their gifts — cheap cloth and coral beads — and dismissed them. But the sea route was now open. Within decades, Portuguese cannon fire would dominate Indian Ocean trade routes that Arab, Persian, and Indian merchants had controlled for a thousand years.
events.revealBlurb: 20 May 1498 CE — Kozhikode (Calicut), Kerala. Da Gama's route around Africa was guided partly by an Indian navigator, Ahmad ibn Majid, who he reportedly bribed in Malindi. The pepper and spices he brought back to Lisbon were worth 60 times the voyage's cost.

events.title: Shah Jahan Commands the Taj Mahal's Construction
events.blurb: A Mughal emperor, grief-stricken after his favourite wife died during her 14th childbirth, commissioned a mausoleum on the banks of the Yamuna at Agra. Over 20,000 workers from India, Persia, and the Ottoman Empire spent two decades shaping white marble into what many consider the world's finest building. The main dome was completed in 1648; the surrounding complex was finished five years later.
events.revealBlurb: 1632 CE — Shah Jahan. The emperor himself was later imprisoned in Agra Fort by his own son Aurangzeb, and spent his final years gazing at the Taj from a window across the river. Symmetry, in the end, was crueller than marble.

events.title: The Taj Mahal Complex is Completed
events.blurb: Twenty-one years after construction began, the final elements of a riverside mausoleum complex — the mosque, the guesthouse, the great gateway, and the formal garden — were finished at Agra. The main dome of the central tomb had been completed five years earlier in 1648. The complex employed 20,000 workers and used marble inlaid with 28 varieties of semi-precious stones sourced from as far as Sri Lanka and Afghanistan.
events.revealBlurb: 1653 CE — Agra, Mughal Empire. Shah Jahan, who built it, was imprisoned in the Agra Fort across the river by his son Aurangzeb five years later. He reportedly spent his remaining years staring at the Taj from his marble window. The reflection pool was designed so he could see it even lying down.

events.title: The Marathas Are Defeated at the Third Battle of Panipat
events.blurb: A Maratha army of 45,000 soldiers and 200,000 camp followers — including families who had brought their children on what they expected to be a triumphant northern campaign — faced an Afghan force under the Durrani king. After an eight-month standoff that left the Marathas starving, they were crushed in a single morning. Between 60,000 and 70,000 troops died in the battle; up to 40,000 prisoners were massacred the following day.
events.revealBlurb: January 14, 1761 — Ahmad Shah Durrani vs. Sadashivrao Bhau, Panipat. Fought on the same plain as two earlier world-changing battles. The Maratha defeat ended Hindu imperial ambitions and opened India to British expansion. It is said that barely a family in the Deccan was not in mourning afterward.

events.title: Hotmail Launched
events.blurb: Two engineers launched the world's first free web-based email service, deliberately choosing the launch date to coincide with a major American holiday celebrating independence. Users for the first time could access their email from any computer with a browser, independent of any particular ISP or employer. The service picked up a million users in six months.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1996 — Sabeer Bhatia and Jack Smith. They chose Independence Day to symbolize freedom from ISP lock-in. Microsoft acquired the service for $400 million 18 months later; it evolved into Outlook.com.

events.title: Wikipedia Launched
events.blurb: A 34-year-old internet entrepreneur who had been trying to build an online encyclopedia by paying credentialed experts to write and peer-review articles gave up on the slow model and switched to a radical alternative: a wiki, editable by anyone. The new version grew faster than expected. It had more articles in its first year than the slow-model version had produced in a previous eighteen months.
events.revealBlurb: January 15, 2001 — Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger. By 2007 Wikipedia had surpassed Britannica in size and approximately in accuracy. Today's English Wikipedia has over 6.9 million articles, and the full project runs in 340+ languages.

events.title: YouTube Launched
events.blurb: Three former PayPal employees, reportedly frustrated that they couldn't easily share a video of a dinner party or (by an alternate legend) a wardrobe malfunction from a recent sporting event, registered a domain name for a video-sharing site. The site's first uploaded video, "Me at the zoo," was an 18-second clip of one of the founders standing in front of elephants at the San Diego Zoo. Google bought them for $1.65 billion in stock twenty months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 2005 — Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, Jawed Karim. The "Me at the zoo" video is still online, with over 350 million views. Users now upload over 500 hours of video every minute.

events.title: Netflix Launches Streaming
events.blurb: A decade-old Silicon Valley mail-order DVD rental company launched an online video-streaming service, initially offering subscribers limited hours of instant streaming on top of their physical DVD subscriptions. The library at launch had about 1,000 titles and required Internet Explorer. The service would eventually make the DVD operation so irrelevant that the company's own name became an anachronism (net-flicks via mail).
events.revealBlurb: January 16, 2007 — initial subscribers got 1 hour of streaming per dollar paid per month. In 2011, CEO Reed Hastings attempted to split DVDs into a sister brand "Qwikster"; the backlash was so severe he reversed within three weeks.

events.title: WikiLeaks Cablegate
events.blurb: A whistleblower-platform website and a consortium of five newspapers began publishing, in coordinated waves, 251,287 U.S. diplomatic cables leaked by a 22-year-old U.S. Army intelligence analyst. The cables ranged from the mundane to the explosive — unflattering private assessments of world leaders, evidence of corruption in allied governments, and revelations about civilian deaths in Iraq and Afghanistan. The leaker would face the longest sentence ever imposed for leaking U.S. government information.
events.revealBlurb: November 28, 2010 — leaker Chelsea Manning (then Bradley), sentenced to 35 years in 2013. Obama commuted her sentence in 2017. WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange lived in the Ecuadorian embassy in London from 2012 until 2019; he was released from UK custody in a 2024 plea deal.

events.title: Octavian Becomes Augustus
events.blurb: The Roman Senate voted Gaius Octavian a new and previously unused title — Augustus, "the revered" — along with broad military command, tribunician power for life, and control of the key frontier provinces. He kept the word "republic" in circulation and called himself only "first citizen," but every structural mechanism of one-man rule was now legally his.
events.revealBlurb: January 16, 27 BCE. Augustus lived another 41 years and died of natural causes at 75 — an almost freakish accomplishment for a Roman emperor. His last words, spoken to friends, were reportedly: "Did I play the part well? Then applaud as I exit."

events.title: Construction of Hadrian's Wall
events.blurb: Emperor Hadrian ordered a stone wall built across the entire width of northern Britain — 73 miles from the Solway Firth to the mouth of the Tyne — with a milecastle gate and two watchtowers every Roman mile. Three legions took six years to complete it; the finished structure included a deep ditch in front and a military road behind, permanently defining the northern edge of Roman Britain.
events.revealBlurb: 122 CE. Hadrian is the Roman emperor who decided to stop expanding and mark permanent boundaries — unusual for an era when conquest was normal policy. The wall was not just defensive; it regulated the movement of traders, taxed cross-border commerce, and projected Roman power into the hills.

events.title: Julian the Apostate's Pagan Revival
events.blurb: Emperor Julian — Constantine's nephew, raised as a Christian — publicly renounced Christianity upon taking power, reopened pagan temples that had been confiscated or closed, restored their revenues, and barred Christians from teaching classical literature in schools. He lasted only eighteen months before dying from a spear wound during a Persian campaign.
events.revealBlurb: November 361 CE. Julian wrote philosophical treatises, got up before dawn to perform sacrifices, and reportedly sacrificed so many oxen that soldiers nicknamed him "the Slaughterhouse." His pagan restoration died with him; every successor returned to Christianity.

events.title: Theodosius Makes Christianity the Sole Legal Religion
events.blurb: Emperor Theodosius issued a series of decrees that outlawed public pagan sacrifice, closed all temples, extinguished the sacred fire of Vesta, disbanded the Vestal Virgins, and ended the Olympic Games. Christianity, which had been a persecuted sect three generations earlier, was now the only lawful religion of the Roman Empire.
events.revealBlurb: 391 CE. The Olympic Games, which had run continuously for over a thousand years, ended because Theodosius considered them a pagan festival — they were not revived until 1896. The fire of Vesta had burned in the Forum for centuries; snuffing it out was treated as a rupture with Rome's foundational identity.

events.title: Permanent Division of the Roman Empire
events.blurb: On his deathbed in Mediolanum, Emperor Theodosius divided the empire between his two sons: eighteen-year-old Arcadius took the east with Constantinople, and ten-year-old Honorius took the west with its capital at Ravenna. No mechanism existed to reunite the two halves, and none ever did.
events.revealBlurb: January 17, 395 CE. Theodosius was the last man to rule the entire Roman Empire. His ten-year-old western heir Honorius grew up to be a notably passive emperor; later historians note that when told "Rome has fallen," he reportedly burst into tears — then relaxed when he learned it was the city, not his favourite hen, also named "Rome."

events.title: Invasion of Poland
events.blurb: At 4:43 in the morning a warship opened fire on a peninsula garrison, and within minutes armoured columns and aircraft were crossing a national border along a 1,600-kilometre front from three directions simultaneously. Two days later, two of the invader's neighbours declared war — and the world's largest conflict had begun.
events.revealBlurb: September 1, 1939 — the battleship Schleswig-Holstein fired the first shots at Westerplatte. The 88-man garrison held out for seven days against a force many times its size. Poland was split between Germany and the Soviet Union by October 6; a government-in-exile continued the fight from London.

events.title: Scuttling of the Graf Spee
events.blurb: A feared commerce-raider that had sunk nine merchant ships in three months limped into a neutral harbour for repairs after a running battle with three smaller cruisers, then sat immobile while international diplomacy set a 72-hour countdown. Twenty thousand spectators lined the waterfront to watch her captain make his final decision.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1939, Montevideo. Captain Hans Langsdorff scuttled the Admiral Graf Spee at 8:55 PM rather than risk his crew in what he believed was an overwhelming British trap. Three days later he wrapped himself in the ship's battle ensign and shot himself. The trap was largely bluff.

events.title: Wannsee Conference
events.blurb: Fifteen senior government and police officials gathered for a 90-minute meeting at a lakeside villa to coordinate the administrative, transportation, and security apparatus required to murder every Jewish person across an entire continent — a project already underway in the east that now needed to be extended westward in an organised and efficient manner.
events.revealBlurb: January 20, 1942, at a villa in the Berlin suburb of Wannsee. The meeting lasted 90 minutes and was followed by lunch. The Wannsee Protocol — the only surviving copy — was found after the war hidden in a filing cabinet. Not a single one of the 15 attendees objected to what was discussed.

events.title: Allied Invasion of Sicily
events.blurb: The largest amphibious operation to that point in military history put 160,000 troops, 3,000 ships, and 4,000 aircraft onto a Mediterranean island in a single night and day — opening the Allied campaign on the European continent itself and within three weeks causing the arrest and removal of a dictator who had held power for two decades.
events.revealBlurb: July 9–10, 1943 — Operation Husky. Benito Mussolini was deposed by his own Fascist Grand Council on July 25, just two weeks after the landings. An elaborate Allied deception operation, "Operation Mincemeat," had planted false documents on a corpse washed ashore in Spain suggesting the real target was Greece — and the Germans believed it.

events.title: Battle of Anzio
events.blurb: 36,000 Allied troops landed almost unopposed on a beach 33 miles south of a major ancient capital, achieving complete surprise — then paused to consolidate rather than advancing, giving the enemy four days to rush in reinforcements and pin the beachhead into a cramped salient that became one of the bloodiest killing grounds of the Italian campaign.
events.revealBlurb: January 22 – June 4, 1944 — Operation Shingle. The initial landing met no resistance; soldiers reportedly bought wine and sat in cafes. Field Marshal Kesselring had the beachhead surrounded within a week. Allied forces took 34,000 American and 10,000 British casualties over four months before finally breaking out. Propaganda claimed "the largest self-supporting beachhead in history."

events.title: Battle of Hastings
events.blurb: A Norman duke from across the English Channel invaded a southern English kingdom with 7,000 men, met its exhausted king — who had marched south after defeating a Norwegian invasion three weeks earlier in the north — on a hillside near the coast, and won in an all-day battle. The English king was killed, reportedly by an arrow through the eye. The victor replaced the Anglo-Saxon aristocracy with his own.
events.revealBlurb: October 14, 1066 — William the Conqueror vs. Harold Godwinson near the town of Battle, East Sussex. The Bayeux Tapestry, a 70-metre embroidered account, was sewn within a decade. Modern English is still 50–60 percent French-derived because of the resulting Norman elite.

events.title: Walk to Canossa
events.blurb: A Holy Roman Emperor, excommunicated by the pope over who had the right to appoint bishops, traveled across the Alps in the dead of winter and stood barefoot in a hair shirt in the snow outside a mountain fortress in northern Italy for three days, begging absolution. The pope eventually let him in and lifted the excommunication. The image of imperial submission to papal authority would haunt European politics for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: January 25-28, 1077 — Henry IV before Pope Gregory VII at Canossa. "To go to Canossa" became a European idiom for humiliating capitulation. Henry later recovered his throne, marched on Rome, and installed his own antipope, so the humbling was strategic rather than spiritual.

events.title: First Crusade Takes Jerusalem
events.blurb: After a month-long siege and a three-year, 3,000-kilometre march from Europe, an army of Frankish knights and footsoldiers breached the walls of a holy city in the Levant and slaughtered its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants indiscriminately over two days — perhaps 30,000 people. The first crusader state was established with a European dynasty on the throne; it would last 88 years.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 1099 — the siege was broken when two Flemish knights scaled a siege tower onto the wall. The leaders competed to be the first to reach the Holy Sepulchre. Godfrey of Bouillon refused the crown of a city "where his savior had worn a crown of thorns" — he was titled "Defender" instead.

events.title: Marco Polo Departs for China
events.blurb: A 17-year-old Venetian merchant's son set out with his father and uncle on a journey across Asia to the court of the Mongol emperor. He would return to Venice 24 years later and, captured in a war with Genoa three years after that, dictate an account of his travels to a cellmate. The resulting book became the most influential western description of Asia for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 1271 — Marco left Venice with Niccolò and Maffeo Polo. Returning in 1295, he was imprisoned by the Genoese; his cellmate Rustichello da Pisa helped him write "Il Milione." Christopher Columbus's annotated copy survives.

events.title: Battle of Agincourt
events.blurb: An exhausted English army, heavily outnumbered, caught in thick mud on a narrow front between two woods in northern France, stood behind sharpened wooden stakes and cut down the armored flower of French nobility with longbows at point-blank range. The French dead included a constable, three dukes, and over 1,500 knights; English losses were perhaps 400. Shakespeare would turn it into a speech 180 years later.
events.revealBlurb: October 25, 1415 — Henry V on St. Crispin's Day. Henry ordered the slaughter of prisoners mid-battle when he feared a rear attack; this remains controversial. The longbow's armor-piercing arrowheads were called "bodkins."

events.title: 15th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: A constitutional amendment prohibiting the denial of voting rights "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude" was ratified, giving Black men the theoretical right to vote. Within three decades, poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, and organized terror had effectively erased Black voting across the former Confederacy.
events.revealBlurb: February 3, 1870. It took the Voting Rights Act of 1965 — 95 years later — to make the amendment's promise practical. Black women were excluded not by race but by sex until the 19th Amendment in 1920.

events.title: 16th Street Baptist Church Bombing
events.blurb: A dynamite bomb planted by Klansmen exploded under the stone steps of a Black church in a Southern city on a Sunday morning, minutes before the 11:00 service. Four girls preparing for choir in the basement were killed; 22 others were injured. The bombing, eighteen days after the March on Washington, hardened national public opinion and accelerated passage of civil rights legislation.
events.revealBlurb: September 15, 1963 — Birmingham, Alabama. Victims: Addie Mae Collins, 14; Carol Denise McNair, 11; Carole Robertson, 14; Cynthia Wesley, 14. The four Klansmen responsible were slowly prosecuted over four decades; the last conviction came in 2002.

events.title: Loving v. Virginia
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court unanimously struck down the laws of sixteen states prohibiting interracial marriage, after a Virginia couple — a white construction worker and his Black and Native American wife — had been awakened in their bed, arrested, and sentenced to a year in jail for being married. The Court called the bans "measures designed to maintain White Supremacy."
events.revealBlurb: June 12, 1967 — Richard and Mildred Loving. They had been legally married in Washington D.C. and returned home to Virginia. Their surname's poetic appropriateness is real, not invented. June 12 is now informally "Loving Day."

events.title: Shirley Chisholm's Presidential Run
events.blurb: A Brooklyn congresswoman, four years after becoming the first Black woman elected to the U.S. Congress, announced her candidacy for the presidency. She was the first African-American to seek a major party's nomination and the first woman to seek the Democratic one. Her slogan was "Unbought and Unbossed." She earned 152 convention delegates before Senator George McGovern won the nomination.
events.revealBlurb: January 25, 1972. She had to sue to be included in televised debates. She survived three assassination attempts during the campaign. "When I ran," she said later, "I ran because someone had to do it first."

events.title: Barack Obama Elected President
events.blurb: A first-term U.S. senator, 47 years old and the son of a Kenyan father and Kansan mother, defeated his Republican opponent by a nine-million-vote margin to become the 44th President of the United States and the first Black person elected to the office. He carried states no Democrat had won in decades, including Indiana and North Carolina.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 2008 — defeating John McCain. Obama gave his victory speech in Chicago's Grant Park before 200,000 people. Jesse Jackson, standing in the crowd, wept on camera. Michelle Obama became the first African-American First Lady.

events.title: Heath Ledger Dies
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Australian actor was found dead in his lower Manhattan apartment by a masseuse who had come for an appointment. The cause was an accidental overdose of six prescription medications, including painkillers, anti-anxiety drugs, and sleep aids. He had recently finished filming an intense performance as the Joker in a Batman film released six months later; his family and colleagues have long disputed the "Joker-drove-him-mad" narrative that emerged. He won a posthumous Academy Award for the role.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 2008 — Heath Ledger in NYC. Daughter Matilda (with Michelle Williams) was 2. His 2008 film "The Dark Knight" was one of the first films to benefit from the surge in digital IMAX releases. His posthumous Oscar made him the second actor ever to win a competitive acting Oscar after death.

events.title: Obama Inaugurated
events.blurb: A 47-year-old former U.S. Senator from Illinois, the son of a Kenyan father and a Kansas mother, was sworn in as the 44th President of the United States on a cold winter morning at the U.S. Capitol. Some 1.8 million people watched from the National Mall — the largest crowd ever gathered in the capital for any purpose. Chief Justice John Roberts flubbed the oath of office so badly that they re-did it privately the following day out of constitutional caution.
events.revealBlurb: January 20, 2009 — Barack Obama. Aretha Franklin's performance of "My Country, 'Tis of Thee" in a famously enormous bow-tied hat became an iconic image. Michelle Obama wore a lemongrass-yellow Isabel Toledo ensemble; she later said it came from a "just make the best of this" impulse.

events.title: Osama bin Laden Killed
events.blurb: A team of US Navy SEALs, helicoptered into the Pakistani city of Abbottabad at night, stormed a walled compound where the founder of al-Qaeda had been hiding for over five years, 1.3 kilometres from Pakistan's premier military academy. He was killed in the raid, along with four others. His body was buried at sea from a US carrier to prevent his grave becoming a pilgrimage site. The president announced the operation in a late-night television address; crowds gathered outside the White House chanting "USA."
events.revealBlurb: May 2, 2011 — Operation Neptune Spear. SEAL Team Six; President Barack Obama. Bin Laden had orchestrated the September 11, 2001 attacks. His death ended a 9-year, 8-month manhunt. The compound was demolished months later by the Pakistani government.

events.title: Kim Kardashian "Breaks the Internet"
events.blurb: A 34-year-old reality TV star and entrepreneur appeared on the cover of a magazine nude, balancing a champagne glass on her bared posterior, with a headline directly daring the internet to be broken by it. The cover image was shared widely enough that the magazine's website crashed for short periods. The photograph — shot by a French photographer who had staged similar images four decades earlier — launched weeks of commentary about sexuality, race, body image, and the limits of viral marketing.
events.revealBlurb: November 11, 2014 — Kim Kardashian on Paper magazine. Photographer Jean-Paul Goude had shot nearly identical images with other models in the 1970s and 80s, drawing accusations that he specifically emphasized and sexualized Black bodies. The cover did, in fact, briefly break the magazine's website.

events.title: Harambe Killed
events.blurb: A 17-year-old western lowland gorilla at the Cincinnati Zoo was shot and killed by zoo staff after a 3-year-old boy climbed through a barrier and fell into the gorilla enclosure. The zoo explained that the gorilla had grabbed the child and dragged him through the water; tranquilizer darts would have taken too long. The killing triggered a wave of online outrage, internet memes, and several years' worth of "RIP Harambe" jokes that became a meta-joke of 2010s internet culture.
events.revealBlurb: May 28, 2016 — Harambe, Cincinnati Zoo. The child recovered fully. The zoo director Thane Maynard defended the decision as the only available option. The Harambe meme's peculiar staying power has been studied as a case of absurdist internet grief; election-poll write-in votes for Harambe persisted for years.

events.title: Prince Charles Marries Diana
events.blurb: The heir to the British throne, 32, married a 20-year-old shy nursery-school assistant at a grand ceremony at a London cathedral. The televised wedding drew 750 million viewers worldwide and unfolded like a fairytale: horse-drawn carriages, a 25-foot train on the bride's silk ivory dress, a balcony kiss at a royal palace afterward. The marriage itself would be miserable; the couple separated in 1992 and divorced in 1996. Both remarried others, and the bride died in a Paris car crash in 1997.
events.revealBlurb: July 29, 1981 — Charles, Prince of Wales and Lady Diana Spencer at St. Paul's Cathedral. Diana tripped on her father's name during the vows ("Philip Charles Arthur George" instead of "Charles Philip..."). Charles, now King Charles III, succeeded his mother Elizabeth II in September 2022.

events.title: Apple's "1984" Super Bowl Ad
events.blurb: A 60-second commercial produced by a British director for a California computer company aired during the third quarter of the Super Bowl. The ad showed a dystopian audience of grey workers watching a Big-Brother-like speaker on a vast screen; an athletic woman in running clothes smashed the screen with a hammer. The product was the Macintosh computer. Apple's board had voted to kill the ad; the CEO insisted it air. It aired once.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1984 — directed by Ridley Scott. The ad ran nationally only that one time; it has since been shown as a promotion or film-clip thousands of times. Macintosh sales in its first 100 days exceeded expectations. The "1984" ad is still considered one of the greatest commercials ever made.

events.title: New Coke Launched
events.blurb: A 99-year-old American beverage company launched a reformulated version of its flagship cola, sweeter and smoother, aimed at winning back market share from Pepsi in a rivalry called the Cola Wars. Blind taste tests had shown a preference for the new recipe; actual consumer response, once they knew what they were drinking, was widespread rage. Letters of protest poured into Atlanta; soda fountains advertised the return of the original. 79 days later, the company announced the comeback of "Coca-Cola Classic."
events.revealBlurb: April 23, 1985 — Coca-Cola. The original formula returned as "Coca-Cola Classic" on July 11, 1985. New Coke eventually became "Coke II" in 1992 and was quietly discontinued in 2002. The whole episode is now a business-school case study in consumer-brand attachment.

events.title: Challenger Disintegration
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch when a rubber O-ring seal on the right solid rocket booster failed in overnight temperatures that had dropped to -8 °C, allowing combustion gases to breach the joint and sever the external tank. All seven crew members were killed, including Christa McAuliffe, who had been selected from more than 11,000 applicants for NASA's Teacher in Space program.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1986 — STS-51-L. Engineers at Morton Thiokol had urged a launch delay the night before, citing O-ring behavior in cold temperatures; NASA managers overruled them. The crew cabin survived the initial breakup intact and fell for nearly three minutes before striking the Atlantic at roughly 320 km/h.

events.title: South Park Premieres
events.blurb: An animated half-hour adult-comedy series about four foul-mouthed 8-year-old boys in a small Colorado mountain town premiered on the Comedy Central cable network.
