The deliberately crude cut-paper animation style and its topical-to-the-minute production timeline (each episode was produced in a week rather than the months typical for animation) gave it a reactive speed no other animated show could match. It would remain in production for over 25 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1997 — created by Trey Parker and Matt Stone. Their earlier Christmas short, "The Spirit of Christmas," had circulated as a VHS among Hollywood executives in 1995. The show's 1999 feature film nearly received an NC-17 rating; the MPAA gave it R after the creators submitted it six times.

events.title: Elizabeth Blackwell Graduates
events.blurb: A 28-year-old English-born schoolteacher, who had been admitted to a small upstate New York medical college as a joke when the all-male student body voted unanimously to accept her application, graduated first in her class to become the first woman in the United States to earn a medical degree. She had been refused admission by 20 other schools. Her younger sister would become the third.
events.revealBlurb: January 23, 1849 — Geneva Medical College, Geneva, NY. No American hospital would employ her; she moved to Paris and London for clinical training. She later founded a medical college for women and practiced for decades, treating patients the profession otherwise ignored.

events.title: Susan B. Anthony Votes
events.blurb: A 52-year-old suffragist and 14 other women presented themselves at a polling place in their upstate New York city and demanded to register to vote, citing the language of the recently ratified 14th Amendment. Three inspectors, after consulting the U.S. constitution, let them register. On election day four days later she voted; she was arrested two weeks after that. Her trial, the following year, denied her the right to testify in her own defense.
events.revealBlurb: November 5, 1872 — Rochester, NY. Judge Ward Hunt fined her $100; she refused ever to pay. The U.S. has since put her face on a coin that was widely disliked and quickly withdrawn (the 1979 dollar).

events.title: Roe v. Wade
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the right to privacy implicit in the 14th Amendment protected a woman's decision to terminate a pregnancy, striking down most state abortion laws. The ruling established a three-trimester framework balancing state interests against individual rights. It would remain the governing precedent for 49 years, until its overturn in 2022 returned abortion regulation to the states.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1973 — plaintiff "Jane Roe" was Norma McCorvey, who never actually had the abortion. She changed her position on the issue multiple times before her death in 2017. The ruling was overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson on June 24, 2022.

events.title: Sandra Day O'Connor Confirmed
events.blurb: A 51-year-old former state senator and state appellate judge from the American Southwest was confirmed by the U.S. Senate 99-0 as the first woman to sit on the U.S. Supreme Court, fulfilling a campaign promise the president who had nominated her made during the 1980 election. She would serve 24 years, writing decisions on affirmative action, abortion, and the disputed 2000 election.
events.revealBlurb: September 21, 1981 — confirmed; Ronald Reagan had nominated her. Her 2005 retirement was precipitated by her husband's declining health from Alzheimer's. She herself was diagnosed with dementia in 2018 and died in 2023.

events.title: #MeToo Goes Viral
events.blurb: Five days after a major U.S. newspaper published a long investigation into sexual harassment and assault allegations against a powerful Hollywood film producer, an actress posted on Twitter asking women who had been sexually harassed or assaulted to reply with two words. Within 24 hours, those two words had been used 500,000 times on Twitter alone. The phrase had been coined a decade earlier by a Black activist working with survivors in the American South.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2017 — Alyssa Milano's tweet; the phrase was coined in 2006 by Tarana Burke. The producer was Harvey Weinstein, finally convicted of rape in February 2020. A cascade of resignations, prosecutions, and cultural reckoning followed across industries.

events.title: Shaanxi Earthquake
events.blurb: The deadliest earthquake in recorded human history struck a densely populated region of northern China in the early morning, collapsing hillsides dotted with cave dwellings carved from soft loess soil. Roughly 830,000 people died — some 60 percent of the population of the affected counties. In some districts, everyone was killed.
events.revealBlurb: January 23, 1556 — Shaanxi Province, Ming Dynasty. The loess hillsides, prized for their insulation, became mass graves when the quake liquefied them. The toll remains a single-event record four and a half centuries later.

events.title: Spanish Flu Pandemic Begins
events.blurb: An unusually lethal strain of influenza, carried through military camps and troop ships during the final months of a world war, infected a third of the planet and killed an estimated 50 to 100 million people in three successive waves over two years. Unlike most flus, it disproportionately killed healthy young adults by triggering cytokine storms in robust immune systems.
events.revealBlurb: March 1918 — first identified at a US Army base in Kansas. It was called "Spanish" only because wartime censorship in belligerent countries suppressed coverage; neutral Spain reported it freely, so it seemed to originate there. It had nothing to do with Spain.

events.title: Great Kantō Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck the main Japanese island at noon, as hundreds of thousands of households were preparing lunch over charcoal braziers. The fires that erupted in the collapsed wooden city were fanned by a typhoon passing offshore, merging into a single firestorm with tornadoes of flame. Around 140,000 people died; 1.9 million were left homeless.
events.revealBlurb: September 1, 1923 — Tokyo and Yokohama. A persistent false rumor that ethnic Koreans were poisoning wells led to vigilante massacres of some 6,000 Korean residents. September 1 is now Japan's Disaster Prevention Day.

events.title: Kobe Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 6.9 earthquake struck a major Japanese port city in the early morning, collapsing expressway sections and igniting fires that destroyed some 7,000 wooden houses. 6,434 people died. The initial government response was famously sluggish — organized yakuza crime syndicates distributed relief supplies before the army arrived.
events.revealBlurb: January 17, 1995 — Kobe. The elevated Hanshin Expressway fell sideways onto its support pillars, a widely published image of post-war Japanese infrastructure failure. The Aum Shinrikyo cult's Tokyo subway sarin attack followed two months later, making 1995 a traumatic year for Japan.

events.title: Tōhoku Earthquake & Fukushima
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the Pacific coast of northern Japan triggered tsunami waves up to 40 metres high that killed some 19,700 people and swamped the seawalls of a coastal nuclear plant. Three reactor cores melted down in the following days, contaminating 337 square kilometres of surrounding countryside. 165,000 people were displaced; many never returned.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2011 — 2:46 PM local time. The quake was so powerful it shifted Earth's axis by about 17 centimetres and shortened the day by 1.8 microseconds. The plant's operator, TEPCO, had been warned about tsunami risk years earlier and ignored it.

events.title: Integrated Circuit Demonstrated
events.blurb: An engineer at a Dallas electronics company demonstrated a germanium chip the size of a paperclip with a working oscillator etched directly onto its surface — the first integrated circuit, combining multiple transistors, resistors, and capacitors into a single monolithic piece of semiconductor. The invention would shrink electronic components by orders of magnitude every decade for the next half-century.
events.revealBlurb: September 12, 1958 — Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments. Robert Noyce at Fairchild developed a similar design independently a few months later using silicon; his is the variant the industry actually used. Kilby won the 2000 Nobel; Noyce had died in 1990 and so was ineligible.

events.title: Sony Walkman Released
events.blurb: A Japanese electronics company released a portable personal cassette player, weighing 390 grams, with headphones instead of a speaker. It had no record function — unusual for a cassette player — and its CEO personally insisted on this as a way of encouraging private, solitary music consumption. The device created an entirely new product category and pulled portable listening out of the car radio and boombox and into the individual's pocket for the next quarter-century.
events.revealBlurb: July 1, 1979 — Sony TPS-L2. Co-founder Masaru Ibuka had wanted something compact to enjoy opera on long flights. The original name in Japan was "Walkman"; in the US, "Soundabout"; in the UK, "Stowaway." "Walkman" eventually won out globally.

events.title: Macintosh Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched a new desktop computer during a Super Bowl advertising spot, and formally introduced it at a shareholders meeting two days later. The machine had a 9-inch black-and-white screen, a mouse, a graphical user interface with icons and windows, and pull-down menus — none of which had previously shipped on a mass-market computer. It cost $2,495 and would struggle commercially against the cheaper IBM PC for years.
events.revealBlurb: January 24, 1984 — Apple Macintosh. Ridley Scott's "1984" Super Bowl ad ran on January 22. The original Mac shipped with 128KB of memory; Bill Gates had quietly promised Steve Jobs a version of MS Word for it.

events.title: Windows 95 Launch
events.blurb: A Seattle-area software company staged one of the biggest product launches in technology history — a billion-dollar worldwide marketing campaign including exclusive use of the Rolling Stones' "Start Me Up," late-night TV appearances, lighting up the Empire State Building, and midnight retail store openings with thousands queuing to buy the shrink-wrapped boxes. The product introduced the Start menu, taskbar, and long file names to mass audiences.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 1995 — Microsoft Windows 95. It sold 7 million copies in the first five weeks. Jay Leno hosted the launch event. The product was legitimately a leap forward over Windows 3.1 — and a reminder that one company now effectively controlled the world's desktop computers.

events.title: BlackBerry Released
events.blurb: A Canadian wireless technology company released a two-way pager with a small keyboard and a monochrome screen that could also receive email. Corporate IT departments loved it — executives could finally stay in touch while traveling — and within a few years the device had become a status symbol and, later, an addiction. Users typed with thumbs on the tiny QWERTY keys; the resulting repetitive-strain injury acquired the nickname "BlackBerry thumb."
events.revealBlurb: January 19, 1999 — Research In Motion's BlackBerry 850. Chosen name because the keyboard's buttons resembled the drupelets of a blackberry fruit. The iPhone's 2007 arrival began BlackBerry's long decline; RIM pivoted to BlackBerry Ltd. and left hardware in 2016.

events.title: First Animal in Earth Orbit
events.blurb: A stray mixed-breed dog named Laika became the first living creature to orbit Earth when the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 2, a 508 kg spacecraft with no reentry capability. Laika survived liftoff and initial orbit but died from overheating within five to seven hours when a thermal regulation system failed — a fact withheld from the public for decades.
events.revealBlurb: November 3, 1957 — Sputnik 2. The Soviets announced Laika died painlessly after several days; the truth wasn't confirmed until 2002. The spacecraft had been built in under four weeks on Khrushchev's orders to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the October Revolution. Laika has since been honored with a monument in Moscow and a postage stamp in more than 70 countries.

events.title: Explorer 1 — First US Satellite
events.blurb: A Juno I rocket launched the United States' first satellite from Cape Canaveral, placing an 8.3 kg cylinder into an elliptical orbit that reached 2,550 km altitude. The satellite's Geiger–Müller tube detected a region of intense radiation surrounding Earth — data that led James Van Allen to identify the radiation belts bearing his name.
events.revealBlurb: January 31, 1958 — Explorer 1. The US had been beaten to orbit by Sputnik 1 and Sputnik 2 in the previous three months. In a press conference photo, three scientists hoisted a full-scale model over their heads in triumph — the actual satellite weighed less than a toaster oven. Explorer 1 remained in orbit for 12 years.

events.title: Skylab Space Station Launch
events.blurb: The United States launched its first space station aboard the final Saturn V rocket, converting a spent upper-stage fuel tank into a 360-cubic-meter orbital workshop. A micrometeorite shield tore away 63 seconds after liftoff, ripping off one solar panel and jamming the other, leaving the station without adequate power and reaching internal temperatures of 52 °C before the first crew arrived and deployed a parasol sunshade.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1973 — Skylab. The station's three successive crews logged a combined 171 days aboard and conducted 2,476 hours of experiments. The last crew staged a work stoppage to protest an overloaded schedule — the first (and only) labor action in space. Skylab fell back to Earth in 1979, scattering debris across Western Australia.

events.title: Mir Space Station Deorbit
events.blurb: Russia deliberately deorbited the Mir space station after 15 years of continuous operation, using three burns from a docked Progress cargo spacecraft to lower its orbit until it reentered the atmosphere over the South Pacific. Most of the station burned up during reentry, but approximately 1,500 kg of debris survived and splashed into the ocean between Australia and Chile.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2001 — Mir deorbit. Mir had been in orbit so long that cosmonauts reported the walls were alive with mold. A Russian company sold pay-per-view rights to watch the reentry from a chartered aircraft. Japan offered to purchase and keep the station operational; the deal fell through over cost. It had been visited by 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations.

events.title: Columbia Reentry Breakup
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Columbia disintegrated over Texas and Louisiana during reentry, killing all seven crew members 16 minutes before its scheduled landing. A 1.2 kg piece of insulating foam had struck the leading edge of the left wing at liftoff 16 days earlier, breaching a reinforced carbon-carbon thermal protection panel and allowing superheated plasma to enter the wing structure during descent.
events.revealBlurb: February 1, 2003 — STS-107. Columbia was the oldest shuttle in the fleet, on its 28th mission. Debris was recovered across 2,000 km of Texas and Louisiana; some experiments in sealed canisters survived, including a container of worms (C. elegans) that lived through the breakup. It was the second shuttle lost in 113 flights.

events.title: Bhagat Singh Executed
events.blurb: Three young revolutionaries were hanged an hour earlier than scheduled at a jail in a Punjabi city, after a three-year trial for killing a British police officer they had mistaken for the superintendent they had meant to assassinate. The youngest of them was 23. Crowds had gathered outside the prison expecting the normal morning execution time; by the time they arrived, the bodies had already been smuggled out and cremated by the riverside.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 1931 — Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, and Sukhdev at Lahore Central Jail. Their martyrdom made them arguably the most venerated revolutionaries of the independence movement, an icon Gandhi's non-violent path never quite matched among the young.

events.title: Gandhi Assassinated
events.blurb: A 78-year-old man, walking slowly across a Delhi lawn supported by two of his grandnieces, was shot three times in the chest at point-blank range by a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for indulging Muslims and accepting partition. He fell murmuring the name of a god. He had survived five previous attempts on his life.
events.revealBlurb: January 30, 1948 — the assassin was Nathuram Godse, a former editor of a Hindu nationalist newspaper. He was convicted and executed. Gandhi had warned his secretary that morning that his life's work would not be judged "until after I am dead and gone."

events.title: Constitution of India Adopted
events.blurb: A constituent assembly of 299 members, chaired by a Bombay-trained lawyer from a once-"untouchable" community, completed two years and eleven months of debate to enact the longest written national constitution in the world — 395 articles, 22 parts, 8 schedules — establishing a secular, socialist, democratic republic. It came into force on the anniversary of a 1930 declaration of complete independence.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 1950 — B.R. Ambedkar, chair of the drafting committee. The date — Republic Day — was chosen because it marked the 20th anniversary of Congress's Purna Swaraj declaration. The final handwritten copy is illuminated by the artist Nandalal Bose.

events.title: Sino-Indian War
events.blurb: Chinese troops launched a sudden offensive across the disputed high-Himalayan frontier in two widely separated sectors, sweeping past overmatched Indian defensive positions within days. Indian morale collapsed; the prime minister broadcast to the nation that "my heart goes out to the people of Assam." China declared a unilateral ceasefire a month later and withdrew to its original claim line, keeping the territory it had wanted.
events.revealBlurb: October 20 to November 21, 1962 — ended with unilateral Chinese withdrawal. Nehru's faith in Asian solidarity was shattered; he died eighteen months later. India rearmed and rebuilt its military, lessons the 2020 Galwan Valley clash showed it had only partially absorbed.

events.title: Emergency Declared
events.blurb: Two weeks after a court had found her guilty of electoral malpractice and barred her from office, a prime minister persuaded the president to declare a state of emergency under the constitution. Opposition leaders were arrested in the night, press censorship imposed, civil liberties suspended, and constitutional amendments rushed through a pliant parliament. The suspension of democracy lasted 21 months and is the darkest interval in the republic's history.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1975 — Indira Gandhi. The Emergency was defended in the name of stability; mass sterilizations, slum clearances, and the personality cult of her son Sanjay made it notorious. Ended March 21, 1977.

events.title: Japanese-American Internment
events.blurb: A presidential order authorised the forced removal of all people of a specific ethnic ancestry from the entire western coast of a country — regardless of citizenship — to inland camps surrounded by guard towers and barbed wire, without trial or individual evidence of wrongdoing. Roughly 122,000 people were displaced; two-thirds were native-born citizens.
events.revealBlurb: Executive Order 9066, signed February 19, 1942. The Supreme Court upheld it in 1944. In 1988, Congress formally apologised and paid $20,000 in reparations to each surviving detainee — roughly 82,000 people. A 2011 Department of Justice memo officially acknowledged the government's lawyers had hidden evidence of innocence from the original court.

events.title: V-2 Rocket's First Successful Test
events.blurb: A 14-metre liquid-fuelled rocket rose from a Baltic coast test site, climbed above the atmosphere, and travelled 190 kilometres before splashing down — the first object built by human hands to reach space, demonstrating a weapon that could strike cities at supersonic speed with no interception possible by any existing technology.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1942, Peenemünde. General Walter Dornberger declared: "This third day of October is the first day of a new era, that of space travel." The same technology later launched the first satellites and moon rockets. The V-2's wartime manufacture killed more people in slave-labour production than it killed as a weapon.

events.title: Battle of Stalingrad
events.blurb: For six months, a city named after a living leader was fought over house by house, factory floor by factory floor, in temperatures reaching minus 40 degrees, as an encircled attacking force slowly starved and froze while its commander received a field marshal's baton and an order never to surrender. The first capitulation of an entire German field army in the war followed 12 days later.
events.revealBlurb: August 1942 – February 2, 1943. Of the 330,000 who entered the Stalingrad pocket, 91,000 surrendered — including 24 generals and Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus. Fewer than 6,000 of those prisoners ever returned to Germany. Hitler promoted Paulus to Field Marshal the day before surrender, noting no German field marshal had ever been taken alive.

events.title: Liberation of Auschwitz
events.blurb: Soviet soldiers opened the gates of a vast camp complex to find several thousand survivors too ill to have been force-marched away, alongside 1.2 million items of women's clothing, 43,000 pairs of shoes, seven tonnes of human hair, and industrial quantities of Zyklon B — physical evidence of the systematic murder of more than a million people.
events.revealBlurb: January 27, 1945. The 60th Army of the 1st Ukrainian Front liberated roughly 7,000 remaining prisoners. The SS had dynamited the crematoria weeks earlier to destroy evidence. January 27 is now the United Nations' International Holocaust Remembrance Day. The surviving Sonderkommando testimonies buried in the ash confirmed what the physical evidence already showed.

events.title: Execution of Mussolini
events.blurb: The founder of one of the 20th century's major fascist movements was captured hiding in a German military convoy while attempting to flee across a northern border, taken to a lakeside village by communist partisans, and shot 26 hours later — his body then transported to a major city and hung upside down at a petrol station for public display.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 1945 — executed at Giulino di Mezzegra on Lake Como, two days before Hitler's death. Mussolini and his mistress Clara Petacci were shot, then driven to Milan and strung up by their heels at the Piazzale Loreto — the same square where partisan hostages had been publicly displayed by Fascists a year earlier.

events.title: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales
events.blurb: An English civil servant in his mid-fifties died leaving unfinished a collection of stories told by pilgrims riding from Southwark to a Kentish cathedral shrine. Written in Middle English rather than French or Latin, the work demonstrated the poetic range of the English vernacular across a social spectrum — knights, millers, cooks, pardoners, the famously bawdy Wife of Bath. Only 24 of a planned 120 tales were ever completed.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1400 — Geoffrey Chaucer. He is often called the father of English literature. Roughly 80 manuscripts survive; the earliest complete ones date from the 1410s. The Wife of Bath's Tale became an early feminist touchstone.

events.title: Pride and Prejudice Published
events.blurb: A 37-year-old unmarried English rector's daughter living quietly with her widowed mother in Hampshire published, anonymously, her second novel — a comedy of manners about five daughters of a small landowner, an arrogant wealthy suitor, and a perceptive heroine who misreads them both. The first edition of 1,500 copies was a modest success; the author made £140 from it. She would die four years later; her anonymity was preserved until a posthumous edition named her.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1813 — Jane Austen, attributed to "By the Author of Sense and Sensibility." She sold the copyright outright for £110; her estate never profited further. Austen is now the most continuously read English novelist. A first edition sold at auction in 2008 for £105,000.

events.title: Ulysses Published
events.blurb: An English-language bookshop owner in Paris published a 730-page Irish novel by a 40-year-old expatriate author that had been serialized, banned, confiscated, and partially burned in the United States. The book followed a single day — June 16, 1904 — in the lives of two Dublin men, using stream-of-consciousness narration that shifted style dozens of times across its 18 chapters. The American mail service seized copies until 1934.
events.revealBlurb: February 2, 1922 — James Joyce, 40th birthday; published by Sylvia Beach at Shakespeare and Company, Paris. The setting day — known as "Bloomsday" — is celebrated by Joyceans every June 16 with readings, pub crawls, and costumed reenactments.

events.title: Things Fall Apart Published
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Nigerian broadcaster published a short novel tracing the life of an Igbo wrestler and farmer in a southeastern Nigerian village and the arrival of English colonial missionaries that destroys his world. Written in English deliberately infused with Igbo idiom, the book pushed back against European literary stereotypes of African societies. It has since been translated into 50 languages and sold over 20 million copies — the most widely read book by any African author.
events.revealBlurb: 1958 — Chinua Achebe. Its title is from Yeats's poem "The Second Coming." Achebe later famously accused Joseph Conrad of racism in "Heart of Darkness." He was in a serious car crash in 1990 that left him paralyzed from the waist down; he continued writing for over two more decades.

events.title: Harry Potter First Book Published
events.blurb: A 32-year-old single mother who had drafted most of the manuscript in Edinburgh cafés over six years, on single-parent benefits, published her first novel after twelve rejections from other publishers. The first print run was 500 copies; 300 went to libraries. Children started reading, telling friends, and returning. Within four years the series had become the most successful in publishing history; she would become the first novelist to reach a billion-dollar net worth.
events.revealBlurb: June 26, 1997 — J.K. Rowling, "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (US title: "Sorcerer's Stone"). Her publisher Bloomsbury suggested using "J.K." instead of Joanne because boys might not read a book by a woman. The series has sold over 600 million copies.

events.title: Pong Released in Arcades
events.blurb: A black-and-white rectangle containing two paddles and a bouncing dot was installed in a Sunnyvale, California tavern as a hardware test. The test machine broke within days — not from malfunction, but because the coin slot had overflowed with quarters. Atari scrambled to ship units nationwide, and the commercial video game industry was born.
events.revealBlurb: November 29, 1972 — Atari Inc., founded that June by Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney, shipped Pong to arcades. The Andy Capp's Tavern prototype jammed after a week because it held too many coins.

events.title: Space Invaders Hits Japanese Arcades
events.blurb: An alien formation that descended one row lower every time a column was destroyed — a quirk of the hardware clock — accidentally created the defining tension mechanic of arcade games. The game was so popular in Japan that bars converted into dedicated parlours.
events.revealBlurb: July 1978 — Taito released Space Invaders in Japan. The Atari 2600 home port in 1980 quadrupled console sales that year. The "yen coin shortage" is an urban legend — numismatists have found no evidence in mint records.

events.title: Final Fantasy VII Released in Japan
events.blurb: A Japanese role-playing game with pre-rendered 3D backgrounds, full orchestral-style music, and a story involving ecological collapse and corporate villainy sold out PlayStation consoles across Japan before it even launched. On release day it sold 1.75 million copies in a single country in a single day.
events.revealBlurb: January 31, 1997 — Final Fantasy VII launched in Japan for PlayStation. It sold 2.3 million copies in its first three days and over 6 million by 1998. Its western release September 7, 1997, introduced the JRPG genre to millions. The 2020 remake sold over 7 million copies in under four days.

events.title: The Sims Released
events.blurb: A game in which you build a house and manage the life of a simulated person — feeding them, making them use the bathroom, watching them catch fire if left unattended too long — became the best-selling PC game of the year, and then 2001, and then the best-selling PC game of all time. More than half its players were women, permanently disproving every assumption the games industry held about its audience.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2000 — Maxis and EA released The Sims for Windows. It sold 1.77 million copies in North America in its first year. The Sims overtook Myst to become the best-selling PC game ever in 2002. The franchise has sold over 70 million copies.

events.title: World of Warcraft Launches
events.blurb: An online game that charged a monthly subscription fee on top of a $50 box price acquired half a million players in its first week and 12 million at its peak — more than the population of several European nations. It swallowed years of people's lives, birthed the term "raiding," generated academic papers about its simulated epidemics, and made "massively multiplayer" a standard genre.
events.revealBlurb: November 23, 2004 — World of Warcraft launched in North America, Australia, and New Zealand. In 2020, researchers cited WoW's 2005 "Corrupted Blood" plague — an accidental in-game epidemic — as a realistic model for studying pandemic behaviour. Lifetime revenue exceeded $9 billion.

events.title: Monteverdi's Orfeo Premieres
events.blurb: A 39-year-old Italian composer staged a setting of the Orpheus myth at a ducal palace in a northern Italian city, combining recitative, arias, choruses, and instrumental ritornellos in a way earlier experimental works had only gestured at. The resulting five-act piece is considered the first opera that remains in the regular performance repertoire. Only two printed scores of the work survive.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1607 — Claudio Monteverdi at the court of the Gonzagas in Mantua. The orchestra called for some 40 instruments. The character of Orpheus was sung by tenor Francesco Rasi; the audience was tiny — members of the Accademia degli Invaghiti.

events.title: The Rite of Spring Riot
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Russian composer's ballet score, depicting a pagan spring ritual with jagged rhythms, dissonant chord stacks, and primitivist choreography, premiered at a new Paris theatre and nearly caused a full-scale audience riot. Shouts, whistles, and fistfights broke out within minutes; the choreographer had to shout counts to dancers from the wings because they couldn't hear the orchestra. The piece is now considered one of the pivotal works of 20th-century music.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1913 — Igor Stravinsky and Ballets Russes at Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, Paris. Choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky. The Parisian critic Carl Van Vechten reported his seat-neighbour beating rhythmically on his head with his fists in distress.

events.title: Kind of Blue Released
events.blurb: A 33-year-old trumpet player released a five-track album recorded in two half-day sessions in a converted Manhattan church. He had given the musicians — including a young tenor saxophonist he had just hired — only short modal sketches, not written music, and one of the tracks was a single take. The album would become the best-selling jazz record of all time, its influence extending to rock, classical minimalism, and film scoring.
events.revealBlurb: August 17, 1959 — Miles Davis at 30th Street Studio, NYC. Sidemen: John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, Bill Evans, Paul Chambers, Jimmy Cobb. It has sold over 5 million copies in the US alone, received quintuple-platinum status.

events.title: Beatles' Final Public Performance
events.blurb: A four-piece rock band performed without announcement on the roof of their recording company's London headquarters for 42 minutes in near-freezing winter temperatures, drawing a crowd of hundreds in the street below before police ended the show citing noise complaints. The impromptu rooftop set was their last performance together in front of a live audience.

events.title: Dark Side of the Moon Released
events.blurb: An English progressive rock band released a conceptual album about madness, mortality, capitalism, and the passage of time, tracks flowing into each other via tape loops of spoken voices, heartbeats, and cash registers. The cover was a simple black triangular prism refracting white light into a rainbow. The album would stay on the Billboard 200 for 741 consecutive weeks — more than 14 years — a record that has never been approached.
events.revealBlurb: March 1, 1973 — Pink Floyd. Recorded at Abbey Road using then-new 16-track technology and Roger Waters' theatrical sensibility. The album has sold over 45 million copies. The "we don't need no education" band followed eight years later with another cultural juggernaut, The Wall.

events.title: FIFA Founded
events.blurb: Representatives of seven European national football associations — Belgium, Denmark, France, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland — met at a Paris sports association's offices and established an international governing body for the sport. England, which had invented the modern codified game and considered itself the natural authority, declined to attend, joined in 1905, and withdrew multiple times over subsequent decades in petty disputes. The organization would run the World Cup from 1930 on.
events.revealBlurb: May 21, 1904 — Fédération Internationale de Football Association, Paris. Its first president was Robert Guérin. FIFA now has 211 member associations, more than the UN. Its headquarters moved to Zurich in 1932 and have been there since.

events.title: Cassius Clay Shocks Liston
events.blurb: A 22-year-old loud-talking boxer from Louisville, a 7-1 underdog against the seemingly invincible heavyweight champion, danced around his opponent for six rounds, cut him under the eye in the third, and won the world title when the champion refused to answer the bell for the seventh round. He skipped around the ring shouting "I am the greatest!" to reporters who had mostly written him off as doomed. He would change his name to one the world would remember the next morning.
events.revealBlurb: February 25, 1964 — Cassius Clay defeated Sonny Liston in Miami Beach. Clay announced his new name, Muhammad Ali, two days later, having joined the Nation of Islam. He would win 56 of his 61 professional bouts and lose his prime years to a Vietnam War draft controversy.

events.title: Magic Johnson Announces HIV
events.blurb: A 32-year-old Lakers star held a nationally televised press conference announcing he would be retiring from the NBA immediately, because he had tested positive for HIV. The announcement — at a moment when the virus was widely associated with gay men and intravenous drug users — instantly changed public perception of who could contract AIDS. He had learned the result days earlier during a routine pre-insurance physical. He would unretire briefly twice, including to play an All-Star Game and the 1992 Olympics.
events.revealBlurb: November 7, 1991 — Earvin "Magic" Johnson at the Los Angeles Forum. He remains alive and visibly healthy over 30 years later, thanks to antiretroviral therapy. His announcement drove huge increases in HIV testing, awareness, and research funding. He returned to the NBA for a 32-game 1995-96 comeback.

events.title: Brady's Super Bowl LI Comeback
events.blurb: A New England Patriots team down 28-3 to the Atlanta Falcons in the third quarter of a Super Bowl came back to tie, forcing the first overtime in Super Bowl history, and won on a two-yard touchdown run that completed the largest comeback in title-game history. The team's 39-year-old quarterback won his record fifth Super Bowl championship and was named MVP for the fourth time. He would win two more Super Bowls over the following five years.
events.revealBlurb: February 5, 2017 — Super Bowl LI, Patriots 34, Falcons 28 OT, at NRG Stadium, Houston. Tom Brady. The Falcons had to stop themselves from ordering Super Bowl champion merchandise at halftime. Brady was the oldest Super Bowl MVP in history (at the time).

events.title: Kobe Bryant Dies
events.blurb: A 41-year-old retired basketball star, his 13-year-old daughter, and seven other passengers died when their private helicopter crashed into a hillside in thick fog outside Los Angeles while en route to a youth basketball game. The retired player had won five NBA championships, two Olympic golds, and the nickname "Black Mamba" during a 20-year career entirely with the Los Angeles Lakers. The crash prompted an outpouring of mourning around the world.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 2020 — Kobe and Gianna Bryant. National Transportation Safety Board findings attributed the crash to pilot error in poor visibility. His 2017 jersey-retirement ceremony at Staples Center saw both his numbers (8 and 24) raised to the rafters — the only player in franchise history with multiple retired numbers.
